paragraphs: The national majority does not claim to conduct all public business. It is obliged to use the township and county magistrates to carry out its supreme decisions.

I have already pointed out the distinction between a centralized government and a centralized administration. The first exists in America, but the second is almost unknown there. Suppose the directing power of the American communities had both of these instruments of government at its disposal, and joined the habit of executing its own commands to the right of commanding. Suppose that, after establishing the general principles of government, it went down into the details of public business, and that, having regulated the great interests of the country, it could reach into the privacy of individual interests. Freedom would soon be banished from the New World.

But in the United States the majority, which so often shows the tastes and inclinations of a despot, still lacks the more perfect instruments of tyranny. In the American republics the activity of the central government has never yet extended beyond a limited number of objects prominent enough to call for its attention. It has never regulated the secondary affairs of society, and nothing so far has revealed any wish on its part to interfere in them. The majority is becoming more and more absolute, but it has not increased the prerogatives of the central government. Those great prerogatives have stayed within a certain sphere, and although the despotism of the majority may be galling on one point, it cannot be said to reach every point. However far the dominant party in the nation may be carried away by its passions, however ardently it pursues its projects, it cannot make all citizens comply with its wishes in the same manner and at the same time throughout the country. When the central government that represents the majority has issued a decree, it must entrust the carrying out of its will to agents whom it often does not control and cannot direct at every moment. The townships, municipal bodies, and counties can therefore be seen as hidden breakwaters, which check or divide the tide of popular excitement. If an oppressive law were passed, the liberties of the people would still be protected by the way in which that law would have to be put into effect. The majority cannot descend to the details, and (as I will venture to call them) the pettiness, of administrative tyranny. Nor does the people have that full awareness of its own authority which would lead it to interfere in these matters. It knows the extent of its natural powers, but it does not know the added resources that the art of government could supply.

This point deserves attention. Suppose a democratic republic like that of the United States were ever founded in a country where the power of a single individual had previously existed, and where the effects of a centralized administration had sunk deep into the habits and laws of the people. I do not hesitate to say that in such a country a more unbearable despotism would prevail than any that now exists in the monarchical States of Europe, or indeed any that could be found this side of the borders of Asia.
The Profession of the Law in the United States Serves to Counterpoise the Democracy

The usefulness of identifying the natural inclinations of the members of the legal profession—These men are called to play a prominent part in the future society—How the particular pursuits of lawyers give their ideas an aristocratic turn—Accidental causes that may check this tendency—How easily the aristocracy joins forces with legal men—The use of lawyers to a despot—The legal profession is the only aristocratic element that will combine with the natural elements of democracy—Particular causes that tend to give English and American lawyers an aristocratic turn of mind—The aristocracy of America is on the bench and at the bar—The influence of lawyers on American society—Their particular habits as magistrates affect the legislature, the administration, and even the people.

In visiting the Americans and studying their laws, we see that the authority they have entrusted to members of the legal profession, and the influence these individuals have in the government, are the most powerful existing security against the excesses of democracy. This effect seems to me to come from a general cause that is worth investigating, since it may produce similar consequences elsewhere.

Members of the legal profession have taken an important part in all the upheavals of political society in Europe during the last five hundred years. At one time they have been the instruments of those who held political authority, and at another they have succeeded in turning political authorities into their instrument. In the Middle Ages they gave powerful support to the Crown, and since then they have worked as hard as they could to limit the royal prerogative. In England they have formed a close alliance with the aristocracy. In France they have proved to be that class’s most dangerous enemies. My aim is to ask whether, in all these circumstances, lawyers have been swayed by sudden and momentary impulses, or whether they have been driven by principles that are inherent in their pursuits and that will always recur in history. What prompts me to this inquiry is the thought that this particular class of men will most likely play a prominent part in the order of things that the events of our time are bringing into being.

Men who have given themselves especially to legal pursuits take from that work certain habits of order, a liking for formalities, and an instinctive respect for the orderly connection of ideas. These make them naturally very hostile to the revolutionary spirit and to the unreflecting passions of the crowd.

The special knowledge that lawyers gain from their studies secures them a separate station in society, and they form a kind of privileged body in the scale of intelligence. The idea of their own superiority comes back to them constantly in the practice of their profession. They are the masters of a science that is necessary but not very generally known. They serve as arbiters between citizens. And the habit of steering the blind passions of parties in a lawsuit toward their own purposes gives them a certain contempt for the judgment of the multitude. It may be added that they naturally form a body, not through any prior understanding or any agreement directing them to a common end, but because the similarity of their studies and the uniformity of their procedures link their minds together as much as a common interest could unite their efforts.

Some of the tastes and habits of the aristocracy can therefore be found in the character of men in the legal profession. They share the same instinctive love of order and formalities. They feel the same repugnance toward the actions of the multitude, and the same secret contempt for the government of the people. I do not mean that the natural inclinations of lawyers are strong enough to sway them irresistibly, for they, like most other men, are governed by their private interests and the advantages of the moment.

In a state of society where lawyers are prevented from holding in the political world the rank they enjoy in private life, we may be sure they will be the foremost agents of revolution. But we must then ask whether the cause that leads them to innovate and destroy is accidental, or whether it belongs to some lasting purpose of theirs. It is true that lawyers chiefly contributed to the overthrow of the French monarchy in 1789. But it remains to be seen whether they acted that way because they had studied the laws, or because they were barred from taking part in the work of legislation.

Five hundred years ago the English nobles led the people and spoke in its name. Today the aristocracy supports the throne and defends the royal prerogative. Even so, the aristocracy has its own particular instincts and inclinations. We must be careful not to confuse isolated members of a body with the body itself. In all free governments, whatever their form, members of the legal profession will be found at the head of all parties. The same remark applies to the aristocracy, for almost all the democratic convulsions that have shaken the world have been led by nobles.

A privileged body can never satisfy the ambition of all its members. It always has more talents and more passions to satisfy and to employ than it has places to offer. As a result, one usually finds a considerable number of individuals inclined to attack the very privileges that they find impossible to turn to their own advantage.

I do not claim, then, that all members of the legal profession are at all times friends of order and opponents of innovation, but only that most of them usually are. In a community where lawyers are allowed to occupy without opposition the high station that naturally belongs to them, their general spirit will be strongly conservative and anti-democratic. When an aristocracy excludes the leaders of that profession from its ranks, it creates enemies who are all the more dangerous to its security because their industrious pursuits make them independent of the nobility. They also feel themselves its equals in intelligence, although they have less wealth and less power. But whenever an aristocracy agrees to share some of its privileges with these same individuals, the two classes combine very readily, and take on, as it were, the solidity of a single order bound by family interests.

In the same way, I am inclined to believe that a monarch will always be able to turn legal practitioners into the most useful instruments of his authority. There is a far greater affinity between lawyers and the executive power than between lawyers and the people. In the same way, there is a greater natural affinity between the nobles and the monarch than between the nobles and the people, although the higher orders of society have occasionally resisted the prerogative of the Crown together with the lower classes.

Lawyers value public order above every other consideration, and the best security of public order is authority. We must not forget that, although they prize the free institutions of their country highly, they value the legality of those institutions far more. They are less afraid of tyranny than of arbitrary power. As long as the legislature takes it upon itself to deprive men of their independence, they are not dissatisfied.

I am therefore convinced that a prince who, facing an encroaching democracy, tried to weaken the judicial authority in his dominions and to reduce the political influence of lawyers would make a great mistake. He would let the substance of authority slip away in order to grasp at its shadow. He would act more wisely by bringing men trained in the law into the government. If he entrusted them with the conduct of a despotic power that bore some marks of violence, that power would most likely take on the outward features of justice and legality in their hands.

The government of democracy favors the political power of lawyers. When the wealthy, the noble, and the prince are excluded from the government, lawyers are sure to hold the highest positions in their own right, as it were, since they are the only men of knowledge and ability, outside the sphere of the people, who can be the object of the popular choice. If their tastes lead them to join with the aristocracy and support the Crown, their interests naturally bring them into contact with the people. They like the government of democracy without sharing its inclinations and without imitating its weaknesses. From this they derive a twofold authority, from it and over it. The people in democratic states do not distrust members of the legal profession, because it is well known that they have an interest in serving the popular cause. The people listen to them without irritation, because they do not attribute any sinister designs to them. The object of lawyers is not, indeed, to overthrow the institutions of democracy, but they constantly try to give it an impulse that diverts it from its real tendency, by means that are foreign to its nature. Lawyers belong to the people by birth and interest, and to the aristocracy by habit and taste, and they may be looked upon as the natural bond and connecting link between the two great classes of society.

The legal profession is the only aristocratic element that can be blended without violence with the natural elements of democracy, and that can be combined with them advantageously and permanently. I am not unaware of the defects inherent in the character of this body of men. But without this admixture of the lawyer’s sobriety with the democratic principle, I doubt that democratic institutions could be maintained for long. I cannot believe that a republic could survive at the present time if the influence of lawyers in public business did not grow in proportion to the power of the people.

This aristocratic character, which I believe belongs to the legal profession in general, is far more distinct in the United States and in England than anywhere else. It comes not only from the legal training of English and American lawyers but from the nature of the legislation and the position these men hold in the two countries. The English and the Americans have kept the law of precedents. That is, they still ground their legal opinions and court decisions on the opinions and decisions of earlier generations. In the mind of an English or American lawyer, a taste and reverence for what is old almost always goes together with a love of regular, lawful procedure.

This predisposition has another effect on the character of the legal profession and on the general course of society. English and American lawyers investigate what has been done. The French advocate asks what should have been done. The former produce precedents, the latter reasons. A French observer is surprised to hear how often an English or American lawyer quotes the opinions of others and how little he refers to his own, while the reverse occurs in France. There the most trifling lawsuit is never conducted without bringing in an entire system of ideas particular to the counsel employed, and the fundamental principles of law are debated just to win a patch of land by court decision. This giving up of his own opinion, and this complete deference to the opinion of his forefathers, which are common to the English and American lawyer, this subjection of thought that he is obliged to profess, necessarily give him more timid habits and more sluggish inclinations in England and America than in France.

The French codes are often hard to understand, but everyone can read them. On the other hand, nothing is more impenetrable to the uninitiated than a body of law founded on precedents. In England and the United States, legal assistance is indispensable, and the ability of the legal profession is generally held in high regard. Both tend to separate lawyers more and more from the people and to place them in a distinct class. The French lawyer is simply a man with extensive knowledge of the statutes of his country. The English or American lawyer, by contrast, resembles the hierophants of Egypt, for, like them, he is the sole interpreter of an occult science.

The position lawyers hold in England and America shapes their habits and opinions no less. The English aristocracy has been careful to draw into its orbit whatever resembles itself, and it has given members of the legal profession great importance and authority. In English society lawyers do not hold the first rank, but they are content with the place assigned to them. They are, in a sense, the younger branch of the English aristocracy, and they stay loyal to their elder brothers even though they do not share all their privileges. English lawyers therefore blend the tastes and ideas of the aristocratic circles in which they move with the aristocratic interests of their own profession.

Indeed, the lawyerly character that I am trying to describe is found most distinctly in England. There laws are valued not so much because they are good as because they are old. If it is necessary to modify them in some respect, or to adapt them to the changes that time brings to society, people resort to the most unimaginable contrivances in order to preserve the traditional structure, and to maintain that nothing has been done that does not fit the intentions and complete the labors of earlier generations. The very individuals who carry out these changes deny any intention of innovating, and they would rather resort to absurd expedients than plead guilty to so great a crime. This spirit belongs especially to English lawyers. They seem indifferent to the real meaning of what they handle, and they direct all their attention to the letter. They seem inclined to violate the rules of common sense and of humanity rather than depart by one jot from the law. English legislation may be compared to the trunk of an old tree, onto which lawyers have grafted the most various shoots, in the hope that, although their fruits may differ, their foliage at least will blend with the venerable trunk that supports them all.

America has no nobles and no men of letters, and the people are inclined to distrust the wealthy. Lawyers therefore make up the highest political class and the most cultivated circle in society. Innovation offers them nothing, and this adds a conservative interest to their natural taste for public order. If I were asked where the American aristocracy is to be found, I would answer without hesitation that it is not among the rich, who are bound together by no common tie. It sits on the judicial bench and at the bar.

The more we reflect on everything that happens in the United States, the more we will be persuaded that lawyers as a body form the most powerful counterpoise to the democratic element, if not the only one. In that country we see how well the legal profession is suited, by its strengths and even by its defects, to neutralize the vices inherent in popular government. When the American people is intoxicated by passion or swept away by the impetuosity of its ideas, it is checked and stopped by the almost invisible influence of its legal counselors. These counselors secretly set their aristocratic inclinations against its democratic instincts, their superstitious attachment to what is old against its love of novelty, their narrow views against its immense designs, and their habitual delay against its ardent impatience.

The courts of justice are the most visible organs through which the legal profession is able to control the democracy. The judge is a lawyer who, besides the taste for regularity and order that he has acquired in the study of legislation, draws an additional love of stability from the fact that he cannot be removed from his office. His legal attainments have already raised him to a distinguished rank among his fellow citizens. His political power completes the distinction of his station and gives him the inclinations natural to privileged classes.

Armed with the power to declare laws unconstitutional, *a the American magistrate constantly interferes in political affairs. He cannot force the people to make laws, but at least he can oblige it not to disobey its own enactments or act inconsistently with its own principles. I am aware that a secret tendency to reduce the judicial power exists in the United States. Under most of the constitutions of the several States, the government can remove the judges from their station when the two houses of the legislature ask it to. Under some other constitutions the members of the tribunals are elected, and they even have to stand for re-election frequently. I venture to predict that these innovations will sooner or later have fatal consequences, and that at some future time it will be found that the attack on the judicial power has damaged the democratic republic itself.
a [ See chapter VI. on the “Judicial Power in the United States.”]

It must not be supposed, however, that the legal spirit I have been describing has been confined in the United States to the courts of justice. It extends far beyond them. Lawyers are the only educated class that the people do not distrust, so they are naturally called on to fill most of the public positions. They fill the legislative assemblies and they run the administration. They therefore exercise a powerful influence on the making of the law and on its execution. Lawyers are, however, obliged to yield to the current of public opinion, which is too strong for them to resist. Still, it is easy to find signs of how they would act if they were free to follow their own choice. The Americans, who have made such sweeping innovations in their political legislation, have made only very sparing changes in their civil laws, and with great difficulty, although those laws are often repugnant to their social condition. The reason is that in matters of civil law the majority is obliged to defer to the authority of the legal profession, and American lawyers are disinclined to innovate when they are left to their own choice.

A Frenchman, used to a very different state of affairs, finds it curious to hear the endless complaints in the United States about the conservative leanings of legal men and their prejudice in favor of existing institutions.

The influence of legal habits, which are common in America, extends beyond the limits I have just described. Hardly any question arises in the United States that does not become, sooner or later, a subject of judicial debate. All parties are therefore obliged to borrow the ideas, and even the language, used in judicial proceedings in their daily controversies. Since most public men are or have been legal practitioners, they bring the customs and technicalities of their profession into the affairs of the country. The jury spreads this habit to all classes. The language of the law thus becomes, in some measure, a common tongue. The spirit of the law, which is born in the schools and courts of justice, gradually passes beyond their walls into the heart of society, where it descends to the lowest classes, so that the whole people take on the habits and tastes of the magistrate. The lawyers of the United States form a party that is little feared and scarcely noticed. It has no badge of its own, it adapts itself very flexibly to the demands of the time, and it accommodates itself to all the movements of the social body. But this party extends over the whole community and penetrates into all classes of society. It acts on the country imperceptibly, but it finally shapes the country to suit its purposes.
Trial by Jury in the United States Considered as a Political Institution

Trial by jury, which is one of the instruments of the sovereignty of the people, deserves to be compared with the other laws that establish that sovereignty—The composition of the jury in the United States—The effect of trial by jury on the national character—It educates the people—It tends to establish the authority of the magistrates and to spread a knowledge of law among the people.

Since my subject has led me back to the administration of justice in the United States, I will not pass over this point without mentioning the institution of the jury. Trial by jury may be considered from two separate points of view, as a judicial institution and as a political one. If my present purpose were to inquire how far trial by jury (especially in civil cases) helps to secure the best administration of justice, I admit that its usefulness might be disputed. Because the jury was first introduced when society was in an uncivilized state and the courts were merely called on to decide questions of fact from the evidence, it is not an easy task to adapt it to the needs of a highly civilized community, where the mutual relations of men have multiplied to a surprising extent and have taken on the educated and intellectual character of the age. *b

b [ An investigation of trial by jury as a judicial institution, and an assessment of its effects in the United States, together with the advantages the Americans have drawn from it, would be enough to fill a book, and a book on a very useful and curious subject. The State of Louisiana in particular would offer the curious phenomenon of a French and an English legislation, as well as a French and an English population, which are gradually combining with each other. See the “Digeste des Lois de la Louisiane,” in two volumes; and the “Traite sur les Regles des Actions civiles,” printed in French and English at New Orleans in 1830.]

My present object is to consider the jury as a political institution, and any other course would divert me from my subject. Of trial by jury considered as a judicial institution, I shall say only a very few words here. When the English adopted trial by jury they were a semi-barbarous people. In the course of time they have become one of the most enlightened nations on earth, and their attachment to this institution seems to have grown with their growing cultivation. They soon spread beyond their island boundaries to every corner of the habitable globe. Some have formed colonies, others independent states. The mother country has kept its monarchical constitution, while many of its offspring have founded powerful republics. But wherever the English have been, they have boasted of the privilege of trial by jury. *c They have established it, or hastened to re-establish it, in all their settlements. A judicial institution that wins the approval of a great people for so long a series of ages, that is zealously renewed at every stage of civilization, in all the climates of the earth and under every form of human government, cannot be contrary to the spirit of justice. *d

c [ All English and American jurists agree on this point. Mr. Story, a judge of the Supreme Court of the United States, speaks in his “Treatise on the Federal Constitution” of the advantages of trial by jury in civil cases: “The inestimable privilege of a trial by jury in civil cases—a privilege scarcely inferior to that in criminal cases, which is counted by all persons to be essential to political and civil liberty. . . .” (Story, book iii., chap. xxxviii.)]
d [ If it were our task to point out the usefulness of the jury as a judicial institution here, much could be said, and the following arguments, among others, could be put forward:

By bringing the jury into the business of the courts, you can reduce the number of judges, which is a very great advantage. When judges are very numerous, death is constantly thinning the ranks of the judicial officials and leaving places open for newcomers. The ambition of the magistrates is therefore continually stirred up, and they are naturally made dependent on the will of the majority, or of the individual who fills the vacant appointments. The officers of the court then rise like the officers of an army. This state of things is entirely contrary to the sound administration of justice and to the intentions of the legislator. The office of a judge is made irremovable so that he may remain independent. But what good is it to protect his independence if he is tempted to sacrifice it of his own accord? When judges are very numerous, many of them must necessarily be unable to perform their important duties, for a great magistrate is a man of no common powers. I am inclined to believe that a half-educated tribunal is the worst of all instruments for achieving the aims that courts of justice exist to serve. For my own part, I would rather submit the decision of a case to ignorant jurors guided by a skillful judge than to judges, a majority of whom are imperfectly acquainted with jurisprudence and with the laws.]

I turn away, however, from this side of the subject. To look at the jury as a merely judicial institution is to take a very narrow view of it. However great its influence on the decisions of the law courts, that influence matters far less than the powerful effects it has on the fate of the whole community. The jury is above all a political institution, and only by regarding it in that light can we appreciate it properly.

By the jury I mean a certain number of citizens chosen at random and given a temporary right of judging. Trial by jury, as applied to the repression of crime, appears to me to bring an eminently republican element into the government, for the following reasons:

The institution of the jury may be aristocratic or democratic, depending on the class of society from which the jurors are drawn. But it always keeps its republican character, because it puts the real direction of society in the hands of the governed, or of a part of the governed, instead of leaving it under the authority of the government. Force is only ever a passing element of success, and after force comes the idea of right. A government that could only crush its enemies on a battlefield would very soon be overthrown. The true sanction of political laws lies in penal legislation, and if that sanction is lacking, the law will sooner or later lose its force. Whoever punishes breaches of the law is therefore the real master of society. Now, the institution of the jury lifts the people itself, or at least a class of citizens, onto the bench of judicial authority. It follows that the jury gives the people, or that class of citizens, the direction of society. *e

e [ An important remark must, however, be made. Trial by jury undoubtedly gives the people a general control over the actions of citizens, but it does not provide the means of exercising this control in every case, or with absolute authority. When an absolute monarch has the right to try offenses through his representatives, the fate of the prisoner is, as it were, decided beforehand. But even if the people were predisposed to convict, the way the jury is composed and the fact that it is not held responsible would still offer some chances favorable to the protection of innocence.]

In England the jury is drawn from the aristocratic part of the nation. *f The aristocracy makes the laws, applies them, and punishes every violation of them. Everything rests on a consistent footing, and England may truly be called an aristocratic republic. In the United States the same system is applied to the whole people. Every American citizen can be an elector and a juror, and can hold office. *g The jury system, as Americans understand it, seems to me as direct and as extreme a consequence of the sovereignty of the people as universal suffrage. These two institutions are instruments of equal power, and both serve the supremacy of the majority. Every sovereign who has chosen to govern by his own authority, and to direct society instead of following its direction, has destroyed or weakened the jury. The monarchs of the House of Tudor sent to prison jurors who refused to convict, and Napoleon had his agents select them.
f [ [This may be true to some extent of special juries, but not of common juries. The author seems not to have been aware that the qualifications of jurors in England vary exceedingly.]]
g [ See Appendix, Q.]

However clear most of these truths may seem, they do not win universal assent, and in France, at least, the institution of trial by jury is still very imperfectly understood. When the question of the proper qualifications of jurors arises, it is confined to a discussion of the intelligence and knowledge of the citizens who may be called, as if the jury were merely a judicial institution. This appears to me the least important part of the subject. The jury is above all a political institution. It must be regarded as one form of the sovereignty of the people. When that sovereignty is rejected, the jury must be rejected too, or else adapted to the laws by which that sovereignty is established. The jury is that portion of the nation to which the execution of the laws is entrusted, just as the Houses of Parliament are the part of the nation that makes the laws. For society to be governed with consistency and uniformity, the list of citizens qualified to serve on juries must grow and shrink with the list of electors. This I hold to be the point of view most worthy of the legislator’s attention, and all that remains is merely secondary.

I am so entirely convinced that the jury is above all a political institution that I still consider it in this light when it is applied in civil cases. Laws are always unstable unless they are founded on the customs of a nation. Customs are the only durable and resisting power in a people. When the jury is reserved for criminal offenses, the people see its action only occasionally, in certain particular cases. The ordinary course of life goes on without its interference, and it is considered an instrument, but not the only instrument, for obtaining justice. This is true all the more when the jury is applied only to certain criminal cases.

When, on the contrary, the influence of the jury extends to civil cases, its application is constantly visible. It affects all the interests of the community, and everyone takes part in its work. It thus penetrates into all the usages of life, it shapes the human mind to its particular forms, and it gradually becomes associated with the very idea of justice.

The institution of the jury, if confined to criminal cases, is always in danger. But once it is introduced into civil proceedings, it defies the attacks of time and of men. If it had been as easy to remove the jury from the customs of the English as from their laws, it would have perished under Henry VIII and Elizabeth, and the civil jury did in fact save the liberties of the country at that time. However the jury is applied, it cannot fail to have a powerful influence on the national character, but this influence is enormously increased when it is introduced into civil cases. The jury, and especially the jury in civil cases, serves to communicate the spirit of the judges to the minds of all the citizens, and this spirit, with the habits that go with it, is the soundest preparation for free institutions. It fills all classes with respect for the thing judged and with the idea of right. If these two elements are removed, the love of independence is reduced to a merely destructive passion. The jury teaches men to practice fairness, and every man learns to judge his neighbor as he would himself be judged. This is especially true of the jury in civil cases, because while the number of people who have reason to fear a criminal prosecution is small, everyone is liable to have a civil action brought against him. The jury teaches every man not to shrink from the responsibility of his own actions, and gives him that manly confidence without which political virtue cannot exist. It gives each citizen a kind of magistracy. It makes all of them feel the duties they are bound to discharge toward society and the part they take in the government. By obliging men to turn their attention to affairs that are not exclusively their own, it rubs off the individual egotism that is the rust of society.

The jury does more than anything else to form the judgment and to increase the natural intelligence of a people, and this is, in my opinion, its greatest advantage. It may be seen as a free public school that is always open. In it every juror learns to exercise his rights and talks daily with the most learned and educated members of the upper classes. He becomes familiar in practice with the laws of his country, which the efforts of the bar, the advice of the judge, and even the passions of the parties make accessible to his understanding. I think the practical intelligence and political good sense of the Americans are largely due to their long use of the jury in civil cases. I do not know whether the jury is useful to those who are in litigation, but I am certain it greatly benefits those who decide the litigation, and I regard it as one of the most effective means of educating the people that society can employ.
